accumulate

/uh-KYOO-myuh-layt/ - the stress falls on KYOO · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Accumulate means to build up little by little — to gather and grow, addition by addition, over time.

Snow accumulated on the fire escape all afternoon, a dry inch an hour, until the railing wore a thick white sleeve.

Example

Priya answered nothing during her six-month sabbatical, and her inbox told the story with a straight face: messages accumulated at about forty a day — no single morning remarkable, no single sender to blame — until eleven thousand of them sat waiting between her and her first day back.

Accumulate is the right word because nothing arrived in a flood; the pile assembled itself an addition at a time, the way accumulation always works. Interest, dust, evidence, and email all obey the same law — small, steady increments that quietly become a mountain.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

amass: to build up a great store, usually on purpose — fortunes, armies, and archives get amassed. Accumulate is quieter and more patient: it works addition by addition, and the pile can grow with nobody intending it at all.

hoard: to stash a supply away and guard it from use — hoarding is about the keeping, with a fist closed over the pile. Accumulating is about the growing; what accumulates may be spent, shoveled, or deleted tomorrow.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

deplete: to use up bit by bit until little remains

squander: to scatter or spend wastefully

Where it sits · how large and purposeful the pile grows

collect → accumulate → stockpile

collect vs. accumulate: Collect is lighter than accumulate: you collect a few shells in one afternoon and the gathering ends, while accumulating is the slow pile that keeps growing for months or years.

stockpile vs. accumulate: Stockpile goes further than accumulate: what merely accumulates can pile up on its own, but a stockpile is built deliberately, crate by crate, against a future need.

Which word fits?

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ac-: toward (Latin ad-, reshaped before c)

Root — cumul-: heap (Latin cumulus)

Suffix — -ate: to make or do — verb-maker

Put it together: Ac- (toward) + cumul- (heap — Latin cumulus, the same heap that names the piled summer cloud) + -ate (verb-maker) = 'to heap up.' The cloud and the clutter grow the same way: a little more, a little more, until the sky or the garage is full.

Use the root in a new word: cumulative: Exam scores matter less than the cumulative record, the registrar reminded them.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral — the word of interest, dust, and evidence

Accumulate is the patient verb of the family, and often nobody is doing it on purpose: leaves, debts, and unread messages accumulate on their own. Amass wants an ambitious subject building a great store; hoard adds secrecy and a closed fist over the pile. When the SAT shows you growth by quiet increments — interest compounding, sediment settling — accumulate is the claim that fits.
